clue.text: Ah, me, that's quick work, if boring

definitions.meaning: an old cry of sorrow, like 'alas'
boring a well in a day would be fast going

explanation.surface: Someone sighs that a job was done fast, provided it was dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like 'dull' but means drilling: sinking a well in just a day is quick work.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic exclamation of grief or regret, close to 'alas', and punningly a well dug in a day.

clue.text: Wind veers two points on the Mersey

indicators.note: a wind that veers changes direction, so its letters change order

parts.note: E and S, east and south, are two compass points

explanation.surface: Wind shifts between compass points over the Mersey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'veers' rearranges WIND into WIDN. The Mersey is the river through Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: Widnes is a town in Cheshire lying on the north bank of the river.

clue.text: How to reduce the men to a thousand

parts.note: M is the Roman thousand; the word men with its last two letters taken away leaves just M, so 'less' those two letters is the instruction

explanation.surface: A grim plan for cutting the workforce down to a thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as LESS EN: take EN away from 'the men' and only M, Roman numeral for a thousand, is left.
explanation.definitionFit: To lessen something is to make it smaller or diminish it.

clue.text: -A defence point with one or another one is with reason 'stronger

parts.note: a fort is a defended stronghold
I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written
another Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A military position with a soldier or two supposedly has a stronger case.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition translates the Latin phrase, which logicians use for 'with stronger reason'.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for 'from the stronger', used when a conclusion follows with even greater force.

clue.text: Everyone including divers

parts.note: divers here is the old word for various, so the phrase means everybody of every kind

explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' suggests swimmers, but it is the archaic adjective meaning sundry or various.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means everybody without exception, of all sorts.

clue.text: Pie ruined by muddled account-sickening!

indicators.note: a ruined pie is broken up, so its letters are rearranged
a muddled set of letters is jumbled, so this abbreviation is mixed up

explanation.surface: A spoiled pie and a confused bill make someone feel ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges PIE into IPE; 'muddled' rearranges ACC into CAC.
explanation.definitionFit: Ipecac is a root extract given as an emetic, a drug that makes the patient vomit.

clue.text: Goes regularly to and fro- in layers

definitions.meaning: a ferry or tradesman that travels a route repeatedly works it

explanation.surface: Something shuttles back and forth in strata.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship plying a route travels it regularly; also thicknesses, as in three-ply wool.

clue.text: Constance Green's a good missionary

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for what such a person does: wins people to the faith

parts.note: Con is a short form of the name Constance
vert is heraldic green, and the possessive adds S

explanation.surface: A woman named Constance Green is said to be an effective evangelist.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'a good missionary converts': the definition is the subject of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A successful evangelist wins people over to a new faith, bringing them round.

clue.text: Perhaps it's in the hunt we get beat

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a chase is a hunt

indicators.note: suggests the short word after it may appear in another order

explanation.surface: A rider supposes it is out with the hunt that one gets thrashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' looks like a hedge on the surface but is the anagram signal for the short word; 'in' is the container signal. 'Beat' is the verb thrash, not a rhythm.
explanation.definitionFit: To chastise is to punish, especially by thrashing.

clue.text: Sped wildly with lubricants in sacks

indicators.note: moving wildly suggests disorder, so the letters of the word before are scrambled

parts.note: oils are lubricants

explanation.surface: Someone races recklessly carrying oils in bags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wildly' rearranges SPED into DESP. 'Sacks' looks like bags, but it is the verb meaning plunders.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack a town is to plunder it, the same as to loot or ravage it.

clue.text: Colourful burnt quarter in Italian city

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the middle of the other

parts.note: Siena is a city in Tuscany
N, north, is one of the compass quarters

explanation.surface: A scorched district of a Tuscan town catches the eye.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the phrase completed by the answer: 'burnt sienna' is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Burnt sienna is a reddish-brown pigment, named after the earth of the Tuscan city.

clue.text: Butterflies-or serpents symbolizing eternity?

definitions.meaning: a family of large butterflies with tailed hind wings
the ancient emblem of eternity is a snake devouring its own tail

explanation.surface: Butterflies, or perhaps snakes that stand for everlasting life.
explanation.walkthrough: The ouroboros, a snake eating its tail, is an old emblem of eternity.
explanation.definitionFit: Butterflies named for their forked hind wings; and literally snakes that gulp their own tails, the eternity emblem.

clue.text: Occurrence remarked about in 'seventeen

indicators.note: the word is said to sit inside the quoted text, so look for it within those letters

explanation.surface: Something that happened is mentioned in connection with a seventeenth item.
explanation.definitionFit: An event is a happening, something that takes place.

clue.text: What's put to bed in Fleet Street ?

definitions.text: What's put to bed in Fleet Street ?

parts.words: What's put to bed in Fleet Street ?
parts.note: in newspaper slang a paper is 'put to bed' when it is finalised for printing; Fleet Street was the home of London's press

explanation.walkthrough: 'Put to bed' suggests sleep, but printers use it for sending an edition to press. Fleet Street is the London street where British national newspapers were based.
explanation.definitionFit: A printed news publication is what printers send to press, or 'put to bed'.

clue.text: Sidon Slate Co broke, merges

indicators.note: a broken company falls apart, so the letters of these three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A slate firm from Sidon goes bust and amalgamates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broke' rearranges SIDON, SLATE and CO together; the surface makes it a bankrupt firm.
explanation.definitionFit: To consolidate is to combine several things into one, as merging does.

clue.text: I would turn to Edmund for a distributor

indicators.note: turning the contraction round reads its letters backwards

parts.note: I'd is the contraction of I would
Edmund Spenser was the Elizabethan poet of The Faerie Queene

explanation.surface: Someone would switch to Edmund as a supplier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses the contraction; Edmund Spenser was the Elizabethan poet of The Faerie Queene.
explanation.definitionFit: A dispenser hands out or deals out goods, so it distributes them.

clue.text: Neglect nothing on the errand

parts.note: O, the figure zero, means nothing
a mission is an errand or assignment

explanation.surface: Ignore nothing while on the task.
explanation.definitionFit: An omission is a failure to do something, a piece of neglect.

clue.text: John involved Ned in fire-raising

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: arson is the crime of fire-raising

indicators.note: involved means tangled, so the name's letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: John got Ned mixed up in setting fires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' scrambles the name and 'in' places it inside. 'John' is defined only by a famous pairing: Burns's song 'John Anderson, my jo', or the wartime Home Secretary of air-raid shelter fame.
explanation.definitionFit: A surname paired with John in Burns's song and in the wartime Home Secretary of shelter fame.

clue.text: Has no mouse in? Perhaps thanks to descendant of Whittington's cat

definitions.text: thanks to descendant of Whittington's cat

indicators.note: signals that the words before may be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A grand house is rid of mice, perhaps owing to an heir of Dick Whittington's famous cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges HAS NO MOUSE IN. Dick Whittington, Lord Mayor of London in legend, made his fortune through his cat; the Mansion House is the London residence of the Lord Mayor, his successor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lord Mayor's official residence in the City of London, home of Whittington's successors.

clue.text: Self-possession with which father returns to see the doctor

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: pa is father
lo is an old word meaning see or behold
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: With composure, Dad comes back to see the physician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' makes PA into AP.
explanation.definitionFit: Aplomb is calm self-assurance or poise.

clue.text: Offspring of Anguilla king among the little people

indicators.note: one letter is set among the others

parts.note: elves are the little people of folklore
R is short for Rex, king

explanation.surface: The children of a Caribbean island's king live among fairies.
explanation.walkthrough: Anguilla looks like the Caribbean island but is the genus name of the eel.
explanation.definitionFit: Elvers are young eels, the young of the genus to which the common eel belongs.

clue.text: Pest officers are suspicious '3, 1,

parts.note: officials who hunt vermin would naturally pick up the scent of a rodent; the idiom for being suspicious says the same

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, rat-catchers detect a rodent by smell; the idiom means to suspect something is wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to sense trickery or wrongdoing, which is what suspicious people do.

clue.text: I entered college after the colonel left, my lord

indicators.note: a letter goes into the middle of what remains
the colonel has gone away, so his abbreviation is removed

parts.note: Col is the abbreviation for colonel

explanation.surface: I got into college once the colonel had departed, sir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' removes the colonel's abbreviation from the word, and 'entered' slips the I inside what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A liege is a feudal lord to whom allegiance is owed.

clue.text: Out with some terrible expletive!

indicators.note: a terrible state is a mess, so these letters are rearranged
only part of the following word is used, its opening stretch

explanation.surface: Someone blurts out a shocking swear word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' takes EXPLE from the start of 'expletive'; 'terrible' rearranges those letters. 'Out with' is an imperative, as in 'out with him!'.
explanation.definitionFit: To expel someone is to throw them out, as the command 'out with him' demands.

clue.text: In backing favourites you need something in a sock

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: pets are favourites, as in teacher's pet

explanation.surface: A punter backs the favourites, and you need something inside your sock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns PETS into STEP. 'Backing favourites' looks like betting.
explanation.definitionFit: The arched middle of the foot, and the matching part of a sock covering it.

clue.text: Lively range of old movie

parts.note: bio- is the prefix of life, so it stands for lively
scope means range or extent

explanation.surface: A vibrant span of an early film.
explanation.definitionFit: Bioscope was an early name for a cinema or film projector, and in South Africa for the movies.

clue.text: Girl-unaffected by setback in France

parts.note: Nan is a girl's name, short for Ann

indicators.note: means the letters of 'set' are read in reverse

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl untroubled by a reverse while in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setback' must be split into 'set' and 'back', the reversal signal. 'Unaffected by' merely winks at the girl's name reading the same either way.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantes is a city in western France on the Loire.

clue.text: A writer's making assignment

parts.note: a scribe is a writer, and the possessive adds S

explanation.surface: A writer is busy producing a piece of homework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assignment' looks like homework but means attributing: to ascribe is to assign.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascribe something is to attribute it, which is assigning it to a cause or source.
